CLEAN: Psychometrically Consistent Incremental Cognitive Diagnosis under Concept-Space Expansion via Architectural Isolation

Abstract.

Cognitive diagnosis (CD) is a fundamental task in intelligent education that profiles learner proficiency over knowledge concepts. In real-world learning platforms, newly added items continually introduce previously unseen concepts, necessitating dynamic expansion of the underlying concept space. Yet existing incremental CD models assume a fixed concept space, allowing gradients from new items to overwrite historical pathways and induce catastrophic forgetting. More critically, these methods rely solely on soft constraints to preserve historical diagnoses. Such constraints may fail to satisfy the requirement of diagnostic invariance after incremental updates, a requirement known as psychometric consistency in cognitive diagnosis. Therefore, we propose CLEAN (Continual Learning with Expandable and Architecturally Isolated Networks), a novel incremental CD framework supporting concept-space expansion while providing structural guarantees for pointwise invariance of historical diagnoses. Specifically, CLEAN first introduces a strict topological bipartition protocol, freezes historical diagnostic functions and applies deterministic orthogonal column masking to sever gradient interference. Second, to accommodate concept expansion, expandable full-rank branches with micro-variance initialization are deployed to learn novel concepts. Finally, to verify that this architectural design achieves invariance by construction, we formalize Representation Drift (RD) to quantify the perturbation of historical traits. Extensive experiments on three large-scale educational datasets demonstrate that CLEAN achieves zero RD, preserving old-item metrics identically to static anchors through architectural isolation while remaining competitive with or superior to strong continual-learning baselines on new items.

Keywords: 
Cognitive Diagnosis, Continual Learning, Parameter Isolation, Psychometric Consistency

1. Introduction

Cognitive diagnosis (CD) underpins personalized learning in intelligent tutoring systems (ITS), inferring each learner’s proficiency over a structured space of knowledge concepts (Wang et al., 2024). Classical models such as IRT (Reckase, 2009), DINA (de la Torre, 2009), and NCDM (Wang et al., 2020) are transductive: learners and items are represented by free parameters, so admitting a new entity requires global retraining. Generative diagnosis removes this bottleneck by replacing entity-specific embeddings with a shared Generative Diagnosis Function (GDF), which maps a sparse response vector to latent traits in a single forward pass (Li et al., 2026). Both paradigms, however, rest on the same implicit assumption that the concept space remains fixed.

Deployed platforms violate this assumption continually. As curricula extend and new instructional units are introduced, incoming items may involve previously unseen concepts and expand the QQ-matrix column-wise rather than merely row-wise, so the diagnostic topology itself must expand. Existing incremental CD studies remain within the row-wise regime: ICD accommodates new learners and items but explicitly fixes the concept set (Tong et al., 2022), while other studies infer QQ-vectors for new items (Qin et al., 2015), diagnose newly registered learners (Liu et al., 2024), or adapt to shifting task distributions (Wu and Zheng, 2025). Widening the trait layer and fine-tuning is the obvious fallback, yet it allows gradients from new items to overwrite the pathways responsible for generating historical diagnoses, causing catastrophic forgetting (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017) (Branch I in Figure 1).

Continual learning offers several remedies, but they are calibrated to the wrong criterion. Regularization and replay (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017; Li and Hoiem, 2016; Buzzega et al., 2020) reduce drift rather than eliminate it, and replay further requires retaining historical responses, which privacy and storage constraints often preclude. Parameter-isolation methods such as PNN (Rusu et al., 2016) freeze prior columns yet reconnect them through dense lateral pathways, leaving historical and newly introduced diagnostic pathways entangled. More fundamentally, these methods certify retention by aggregate accuracy on old tasks, whereas a CD model is a measurement instrument: if a learner’s reported mastery of fractions shifts merely because trigonometry is introduced into the platform, remediation is misdirected even when average accuracy remains unchanged. CD therefore requires a strict form of psychometric consistency related to measurement invariance (Vandenberg and Lance, 2000), such that historical diagnoses must remain unchanged after incremental updates for the same response input. No soft penalty can guarantee this invariance.

Our key observation is that such invariance need not be enforced through optimization. The expert-annotated QQ-matrix already specifies which concepts each item measures, allowing this topology to be compiled directly into the network. We therefore propose CLEAN (Continual Learning with Expandable, Architecturally Isolated Networks). Its Strict Topological Bipartition (STB) protocol reorders the QQ-matrix into a block-triangular form in which old items never reference new concepts. Guided by it, CLEAN freezes historical GDFs, applies deterministic orthogonal column masking, and freezes the shared aggregation bias, so incremental gradients cannot reach historical pathways, while expandable full-rank or low-rank (Hu et al., 2022) branches capture new concepts (Branch II in Figure 1). Invariance thus becomes a property of the computational graph rather than an optimization objective.

The contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We formulate incremental CD under joint item- and concept-space expansion, and define Representation Drift (RD) to quantify perturbation of historical traits, taking RD=0\mathrm{RD}=0 as one important operational criterion for psychometric consistency.

  • •

    CLEAN compiles the QQ-matrix into an isolation topology via STB and combines frozen historical pathways, orthogonal column masking, and micro-variance-initialized expandable branches, yielding invariance by construction, with a LoRA variant for constrained parameter budgets.

  • •

    On Junyi, ASSISTments, and Math1, spanning dense to highly sparse responses, CLEAN attains RD=0\mathrm{RD}=0 and exactly retains anchor-level old-item metrics, while no baseline surpasses it on new items without either replaying stored responses or incurring substantial representation drift.

2. RELATED WORK

Concept-space expansion imposes two requirements that we use below to position existing work: (i) column-wise expansion of the Q-matrix when previously unseen concepts arrive, and (ii) pointwise invariance of historical diagnoses after such expansion, as demanded by psychometric consistency (Vandenberg and Lance, 2000).

Cognitive Diagnosis Models. By parameterization, CDMs fall into transductive and generative families (Wang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026). Transductive models assign independent parameters to each learner and item, ranging from psychometric formulations such as IRT (Hambleton and Swaminathan, 2013), MIRT (Reckase, 2009) and the Q-matrix-based DINA (de la Torre, 2009), to neural and structure-aware extensions including NCDM (Wang et al., 2020), DIRT (Cheng et al., 2019), RCD (Gao et al., 2021), HierCDF (Li et al., 2022), and KSCD (Ma et al., 2022). Because these parameters are entity-specific, every newly arriving learner or item triggers global retraining. Generative models remove this bottleneck by mapping response logs to proficiency through shared diagnostic functions, enabling immediate inference for unseen learners (Li et al., 2026). Both families, however, are defined over a fixed concept space and therefore meet neither requirement.

Incremental Cognitive Diagnosis. Existing incremental work expands the diagnostic system along entities rather than concepts. Qin et al. (Qin et al., 2015) estimate the Q-vectors of new items from correctly specified base items, which appends rows to the Q-matrix while leaving its columns fixed. ICD (Tong et al., 2022), the work closest to ours, accommodates new learners and items through a deep trait network and a stability-oriented update rule, yet explicitly assumes an unchanged concept set. ICDM (Liu et al., 2024) targets sparse response logs of newly registered learners, and MetaCD (Wu and Zheng, 2025) combines meta-learning with parameter protection under shifting data distributions. None of these methods supports requirement (i), and each preserves historical diagnoses only approximately, through soft stability terms rather than by construction.

Continual Learning and the Measurement of Forgetting. Continual learning mitigates catastrophic forgetting (Goodfellow et al., 2014; Parisi et al., 2019) along three lines. Regularization penalizes changes to important parameters or distills previous outputs (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017; Li and Hoiem, 2016); replay rehearses stored samples or logits (Rebuffi et al., 2017; Lopez-Paz and Ranzato, 2017; Chaudhry et al., 2019; Buzzega et al., 2020; Boschini et al., 2023), which presumes continued access to historical data; architecture-based methods allocate task-specific parameters, either as full columns with lateral connections, as in PNN (Rusu et al., 2016), or as low-rank adapters constrained by soft orthogonality, protected subspaces, and dual branches, as in the LoRA family (Hu et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2025; Liang and Li, 2024; He et al., 2025; Xiong and Xie, 2026). The first two lines suppress drift without eliminating it, whereas the third is driven by task identity and is therefore blind to the concept-level topology encoded in the Q-matrix. Standard evaluation masks this gap: forgetting is typically reported through aggregate old-task statistics such as average accuracy or forgetting scores (Chaudhry et al., 2018; Lange et al., 2022), and drift-aware methods estimate representation shift in order to compensate for it after the fact (Yu et al., 2020). A model may thus retain its aggregate accuracy on historical items while silently altering individual learners’ proficiency on existing concepts, which is precisely what psychometric consistency forbids. Our CLEAN closes both gaps by making historical invariance a structural property of the architecture rather than an optimization objective.

3. PRELIMINARY

3.1. Generative Cognitive Diagnosis Backbone

Let 𝒰={u1,…,uN}\mathcal{U}=\{u_{1},\ldots,u_{N}\}, ℐ={I1,…,IM}\mathcal{I}=\{I_{1},\ldots,I_{M}\}, and 𝒦={k1,…,kT}\mathcal{K}=\{k_{1},\ldots,k_{T}\} denote the sets of learners, items, and knowledge concepts, respectively. Their associations are specified by an expert-defined QQ-matrix Q∈{0,1}M×TQ\in\{0,1\}^{M\times T}, where Qm​t=1Q_{mt}=1 indicates that item ImI_{m} requires concept ktk_{t} (de la Torre, 2009). (2) ui​j=Wθ(θi⊙Qj⋅)+bθ,vi​j=Wψ(ψj⊙Qj⋅)+bψ.u_{ij}=W_{\theta}\left(\theta_{i}\odot Q_{j\cdot}\right)+b_{\theta},\qquad v_{ij}=W_{\psi}\left(\psi_{j}\odot Q_{j\cdot}\right)+b_{\psi}.

where Wθ,Wψ∈ℝd×TW_{\theta},W_{\psi}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times T} and bθ,bψ∈ℝdb_{\theta},b_{\psi}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. The QQ-mask retains only the concepts required by IjI_{j}. The resulting embeddings ui​ju_{ij} and vi​jv_{ij} are then fed into the item response function (IRF).

Response Reconstruction (Item Response Function). The IRF predicts the probability of a correct response from the aggregated learner and item representations:

(3) y^i​j=MLP⁡(ui​j−vi​j)∈(0,1).\hat{y}_{ij}=\operatorname{MLP}\left(u_{ij}-v_{ij}\right)\in(0,1).

where ui​j−vi​ju_{ij}-v_{ij} represents the gap between learner proficiency and item demand, and the MLP produces the predicted response probability through a sigmoid output layer. The model is trained on observed learner–item interactions using binary cross-entropy loss (Li et al., 2026).

3.2. Incremental Cognitive Diagnosis Setting

Let MoldM_{\mathrm{old}} and KoldK_{\mathrm{old}} denote the numbers of historical items and knowledge concepts, respectively. We train the anchor model fΦ(0)f_{\Phi^{(0)}} on 𝒟old\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{old}} with an Mold×KoldM_{\mathrm{old}}\times K_{\mathrm{old}} QQ-matrix, yielding θu(0)∈ℝKold\theta_{u}^{(0)}\in\mathbb{R}^{K_{\mathrm{old}}}.

In open instructional systems, the knowledge concept space and item bank expand continuously as new knowledge concepts and items are introduced. At incremental step tt, the addition of Δ​M\Delta M new items and Δ​K\Delta K new knowledge concepts expands the QQ-matrix to (Mold+Δ​M)×(Kold+Δ​K).\left(M_{\mathrm{old}}+\Delta M\right)\times\left(K_{\mathrm{old}}+\Delta K\right). The expanded model fΦ(t)f_{\Phi^{(t)}} must infer proficiency in the new knowledge concepts and predict responses to the new items while satisfying the representation-level stability constraint:

(4) θu,[1:Kold](t)=θu(0),∀u∈𝒰.\theta_{u,[1:K_{\mathrm{old}}]}^{(t)}=\theta_{u}^{(0)},\qquad\forall u\in\mathcal{U}.

We quantify deviations from this zero-drift condition using Representation Drift (RD) in the following section.

3.3. Quantitative Metric: Representation Drift

Definition of RD. Representation Drift (RD) measures the Euclidean shift in the representations of the same historical learners before and after incremental learning. Analogous to semantic drift in class-incremental learning (Yu et al., 2020), RD quantifies changes in the historical representation space induced by incremental learning. In generative cognitive diagnosis, this space is defined by concept-aligned latent ability traits θ\theta, making RD a trait-space drift metric for the historical diagnostic subspace.

Let 𝒰oldtest\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{old}}^{\mathrm{test}} denote the learners evaluated on the old-item test set. For each learner i∈𝒰oldtesti\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{old}}^{\mathrm{test}}, let θi(0)∈ℝKoldandθi(t)∈ℝKold+Δ​K\theta_{i}^{(0)}\in\mathbb{R}^{K_{\mathrm{old}}}\quad\text{and}\quad\theta_{i}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}^{K_{\mathrm{old}}+\Delta K} denote the latent traits inferred by the initial and incremental models, respectively. The slice [1:Kold][1:K_{\mathrm{old}}] selects the dimensions corresponding to historical concepts. RD is defined as

(5) RD=1|𝒰oldtest|​Kold∑i∈𝒰oldtest‖θi(0)−θi,[1:Kold](t)‖2.\mathrm{RD}=\frac{1}{\left|\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{old}}^{\mathrm{test}}\right|\sqrt{K_{\mathrm{old}}}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{old}}^{\mathrm{test}}}\left\|\theta_{i}^{(0)}-\theta_{i,[1:K_{\mathrm{old}}]}^{(t)}\right\|_{2}.

When RD=0\mathrm{RD}=0, historical traits are pointwise invariant in the old-concept subspace, indicating representation-level consistency. The Kold\sqrt{K_{\mathrm{old}}} normalization reduces dimensionality effects and enables comparison across models. However, RD only captures representation-level stability, while psychometric consistency is reflected in unchanged old-item predictions under the same historical inputs. Achieving the latter additionally relies on Orthogonal Column Masking and Shared Bias Freezing, as shown in Section 5.3.

4. Methodology

4.1. Overview of CLEAN

CLEAN freezes the parameters associated with historical concepts and learns newly introduced concepts through isolated incremental branches. As illustrated in Figure 2, CLEAN integrates STB-based topological reordering, expandable Generative Diagnosis Functions (GDFs), and an architecturally isolated aggregation layer. Historical parameters remain unaffected by incremental gradients, while STB, Orthogonal Column Masking, and Shared Bias Freezing prevent new-concept updates from altering old-item diagnostic pathways. Consequently, CLEAN preserves the historical trait subspace with RD=0\mathrm{RD}=0 and maintains unchanged old-item diagnostic outputs. Meanwhile, the trainable capacity of the incremental branches is devoted to learning newly introduced concepts. The following subsections present the STB protocol, the expandable CLEAN-GDF with micro-variance initialization and separate pathways for learner and item traits, and aggregation-layer isolation through Orthogonal Column Masking and Shared Bias Freezing.

4.2. STB Protocol

STB is a partitioning and reordering protocol operating on QQ-matrix indices. It establishes the topological prerequisites for the subsequent structural partitioning of the computational graph. Given a new knowledge concept set 𝒦new\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{new}}, STB classifies items based on whether they involve any new knowledge concepts.

Specifically, items involving at least one new knowledge concept are classified as new items, whereas those involving only existing knowledge concepts are classified as old items. After the item rows and concept columns are reordered accordingly, the QQ-matrix exhibits a clean block-structured topology:

Q=[Qℐold,𝒦old𝟎Qℐnew,𝒦oldQℐnew,𝒦new]=[Q11𝟎Q21Q22].Q=\left[\begin{matrix}Q_{\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{old}},\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{old}}}&\mathbf{0}\\ Q_{\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{new}},\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{old}}}&Q_{\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{new}},\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{new}}}\end{matrix}\right]=\left[\begin{matrix}Q_{11}&\mathbf{0}\\ Q_{21}&Q_{22}\end{matrix}\right].

There is a sound psychometric basis for setting the QQ-matrix entries between old items and new knowledge concepts to zero: a model trained only on historical stages has never observed any signals related to the new concepts. By enforcing that old items are not associated with new knowledge concepts, the incremental evaluation benchmark remains uncontaminated, ensuring that the forgetting and plasticity metrics for historical items are not distorted by newly introduced concepts.

By contrast, traditional lateral-growth neural network methods (Rusu et al., 2016) do not explicitly distinguish between historical and newly added training data. As a result, the feature information associated with the same knowledge concept may be simultaneously encoded by parameters in both the old and new networks, entangling historical and incremental diagnostic pathways. This entanglement disrupts the historical diagnostic space and substantially undermines measurement consistency.

The core mathematical property of STB lies in the upper-right block, Q12≡𝟎Q_{12}\equiv\mathbf{0}, indicating that historical items in ℐold\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{old}} are not associated with any newly introduced concepts in 𝒦new\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{new}}. In contrast, new items in ℐnew\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{new}} may still involve historical concepts, so Qℐnew,𝒦oldQ_{\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{new}},\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{old}}} can be nonzero. This preserves the authentic topology in which newly introduced items may assess both historical and new knowledge concepts.

The upper-right block topology, characterized by Q12=𝟎Q_{12}=\mathbf{0}, provides the basis for the orthogonal column masking described in Section 4.4.1, enabling simultaneous zeroing in both the forward and backward paths. STB is a partitioning protocol rather than a learnable model component; it defines the topological boundaries between historical and newly added items and knowledge concepts based on expert-annotated QQ-matrices.

By definition, any item associated with at least one newly introduced knowledge concept in 𝒦new\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{new}} is assigned to ℐnew\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{new}}. Consequently, the items remaining in ℐold\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{old}} naturally satisfy the condition Q12=𝟎Q_{12}=\mathbf{0}.

4.3. CLEAN-GDF

As discussed earlier, cognitive diagnosis typically serves as an upstream task for downstream educational applications; therefore, the induced trait representations should remain as stable as possible across incremental updates. We need the predicted traits θ\theta and ψ\psi themselves to evolve smoothly. To this end, we adapt the GDF via a micro-variance initialization scheme for newly grown branches.

Instead of standard Xavier initialization (Glorot and Bengio, 2010), the newly grown network weights are initialized from a truncated Gaussian distribution scaled down by a factor of 10−310^{-3} relative to the variance of the existing parameters. This prevents abrupt disturbances to the established diagnostic space while allowing the new parameters to receive gradients and gradually learn new concepts.

(6) Wnew(a,b)∼𝒩[−2​σ, 2​σ]​(0,σ2),σ=Var⁡(Wref)⋅10−3.W_{\mathrm{new}}^{(a,b)}\sim\mathcal{N}_{[-2\sigma,\,2\sigma]}\left(0,\sigma^{2}\right),\qquad\sigma=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}\left(W_{\mathrm{ref}}\right)\cdot 10^{-3}}.

where each newly grown parameter Wnew(a,b)W_{\mathrm{new}}^{(a,b)} is sampled from a zero-mean Gaussian distribution truncated to the interval [−2​σ,2​σ][-2\sigma,2\sigma].

First, to avoid “zero-gradient death,” new branches are initialized with small nonzero weights. If the weights of a new branch are initialized to zero, both its forward activations and backward gradients become zero, preventing the branch from learning. This issue is particularly severe for LoRA variant (Hu et al., 2022) , where setting both factors in Δ​W=B​A\Delta W=BA to zero causes their gradients to vanish. We therefore initialize A,B∼𝒩⁡(0,10−6)A,B\sim\mathcal{N}(0,10^{-6}), enabling both factors to update from the first mini-batch while keeping the initial contribution of Δ​W=B​A\Delta W=BA near zero.

Second, micro-variance initialization places the newly added full-rank branch in a near-silent initial state: new weights are drawn from a truncated Gaussian whose variance is 10−310^{-3} times that of the frozen reference parameters. Consequently, training starts from a well-conditioned baseline close to the anchor point and gradually accumulates capacity, avoiding large random perturbations at the beginning and leading to more stable convergence.

Importantly, although θ\theta and ψ\psi follow the same micro-variance growth principle, they use separate expansion pathways rather than sharing a common incremental trunk. Learner traits θ\theta are generated by the response-to-ability encoder f⁡(⋅)f(\cdot) and its new branch fnewf_{\mathrm{new}}, whereas item traits ψ\psi are generated by the dual encoder g⁡(⋅)g(\cdot) and its new branch gnewg_{\mathrm{new}}.

For learner traits, each response vector is partitioned into old- and new-item blocks. The frozen encoder foldf_{\mathrm{old}} processes old items to produce θold\theta_{\mathrm{old}}, while fnewf_{\mathrm{new}} processes new items to produce θnew\theta_{\mathrm{new}}. The two outputs are then concatenated along the concept dimension. For item traits, the complete learner-wise response column is fed into both pathways without input partitioning. Likewise, the frozen encoder goldg_{\mathrm{old}} produces ψold\psi_{\mathrm{old}}, while gnewg_{\mathrm{new}} produces ψnew\psi_{\mathrm{new}}. The two representations are then concatenated along the concept dimension and passed to the subsequent aggregation layer.

This asymmetric design reflects the different structures of learner and item response logs. A learner response vector contains interactions with both old and new items, so input partitioning is used to prevent gradients from new items from disturbing historical ability dimensions. In contrast, each item is treated as a single entity, and its diagnostic input is already a complete user-wise response column. Accordingly, the ψ\psi pathway does not exhibit the cross-block interference observed in the learner pathway and therefore does not require the response column to be partitioned into old- and new-item blocks.

4.4. CLEAN Aggregation Layer

The aggregation layer projects the concept-level traits θ,ψ∈ℝK\theta,\psi\in\mathbb{R}^{K} into dense representations in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, which are subsequently fed into the IRF. After topological expansion, the old and newly introduced concept traits are concatenated along the concept dimension. The expanded concept representation is then projected by the same aggregation layer into a fixed-dimensional dense representation for the IRF. If the historical weight columns or the shared bias were allowed to change, even a frozen GDF would no longer reproduce the anchored traits of old items. Therefore, the aggregation layer must simultaneously support plasticity for newly introduced concepts while preserving the historical aggregation subspace in a bitwise-identical state with respect to the foundation-stage anchor. We achieve this through two complementary mechanisms: Deterministic Orthogonal Column Masking for the concept-wise weights (Section 4.4.1) and Shared Bias Freezing for the aggregation bias (Section 4.4.2).

4.4.1. Deterministic Orthogonal Column Masking.

This mechanism is central to achieving pointwise invariance of historical diagnostic outputs. Rather than explicitly applying a binary vector, the mask is implicitly induced at the aggregation layer by the STB structure with Q12=0Q_{12}=0 through two steps: chunk-wise slicing and incremental block de-biasing. For a given item ImI_{m}, aggregation is decoupled across the historical and new subspaces:

(7) agg⁡(m)=Wold​(θold⊙qmold)+bold⏟frozen historical block with bias+Wnew​(θnew⊙qmnew).⏟incremental block without bias\operatorname{agg}(m)=\underbrace{W^{\mathrm{old}}\left(\theta_{\mathrm{old}}\odot q_{m}^{\mathrm{old}}\right)+b^{\mathrm{old}}}_{\text{frozen historical block with bias}}+\underbrace{W^{\mathrm{new}}\left(\theta_{\mathrm{new}}\odot q_{m}^{\mathrm{new}}\right).}_{\text{incremental block without bias}}

For any historical item Im∈ℐoldI_{m}\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{old}}, STB ensures that the columns corresponding to new knowledge concepts are zero, yielding θnew⊙qmnew=0\theta_{\mathrm{new}}\odot q_{m}^{\mathrm{new}}=0. Structurally, the forward prediction for old items contains no contribution from new concepts. Because the historical aggregation columns WoldW^{\mathrm{old}} and the shared bias bb (Section 4.4.2) are frozen at their anchor values, old-item predictions remain identical to those of the anchor model.

This mask is termed orthogonal because it effectively decouples parameter updates between the historical and newly introduced subspaces along the concept dimension. To clarify this property, we distinguish two complementary separation mechanisms. First, the clean forward pass for historical items is guaranteed by STB, where the new-concept columns are zero for historical items. As a result, the new-concept components are always multiplied by zero, independently of the column mask. Second, the column mask operates during the backward pass: it zeroes out the gradients of the historical aggregation weight columns, i.e., [:,:Kold]\bigl[:,\,:K_{\mathrm{old}}\bigr], preventing them from drifting when training on new items that may still involve historical concepts. In this way, the weights of the historical concept columns remain locked at their anchor points. It should also be emphasized that the column mask applies only to weights, not biases. The stability of the shared bias in the aggregation layer is guaranteed by the bias-freezing mechanism described in Section 4.4.2. Furthermore, during the forward pass, the incremental diagnostic branch uses only responses associated with new items, denoted as 𝐱new=user_log[:,Iold:]\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}=\texttt{user\_log}[:,\,I_{\mathrm{old}}:], to generate θnew\theta_{\mathrm{new}}, instead of reusing hidden-layer features from the historical subnet. This design cuts off the coupling chain at its source and ensures that the gradient graph of the frozen historical network remains completely disjoint from that of the incremental branch.

4.4.2. Parameter Bias Freezing.

The aggregation layer contains a shared bias term bb in addition to the weight columns corresponding to historical and new concepts. Since the orthogonal column mask applies only to weights, the bias term bb would still be updated by the optimizer during incremental training if left unconstrained. Therefore, a second layer of isolation is required. To this end, we exclude the shared bias of the aggregation layer from the optimizer and freeze it at the anchor value bo​l​db^{old}, restricting incremental updates to the new-concept branch and the weight columns associated with new concepts. Consequently, for any historical input, the aggregated output remains Wold​(θold⊙qold)+bo​l​dW^{\mathrm{old}}(\theta_{\mathrm{old}}\odot q_{\mathrm{old}})+b^{old}, ensuring bitwise identity with the anchor state. Bias freezing and orthogonal column masking address complementary aspects of architectural isolation and are both indispensable. Removing either mechanism immediately degrades prediction performance on old items, as shown in Section 5.3 and Table 2. Together, these mechanisms lock the entire historical aggregation subspace.

5. EXPERIMENTS

5.1. Experimental Setup

We use three real-world datasets: Junyi, ASSISTments 2009–2010 Skill Builder (ASSIST), and Math1. Junyi is derived from Junyi Academy by selecting the 1,000 most active students, yielding a 712×39712\times 39 QQ-matrix with 71.36% response sparsity, which is used to evaluate model performance under normal interaction conditions. ASSIST, based on the ASSISTments online tutoring system, contains 4,163 students and 17,746 exercises after preprocessing, with a 17,746×12317{,}746\times 123 QQ-matrix and 99.64% sparsity, which is used to evaluate model performance under extremely data-scarce scenarios. Math1, a classic cognitive diagnosis benchmark, contains 4,209 students, 20 exercises, and 11 knowledge concepts, yielding a 20×1120\times 11 QQ-matrix. Its response matrix is fully observed, comprising 84,180 interactions with 0.00% sparsity, which is used to evaluate model performance under extremely interaction-dense scenarios.

Data Split. We use a 70%/10%/20% train/validation/test split. Under the random-split setting, learner–item interactions are randomly partitioned while allowing the same learners to appear in all three sets. This setting isolates incremental item- and concept-space expansion from cold-start learner adaptation. An additional user-split evaluation with mutually exclusive learner groups is reported in Appendix A.1.

Experimental Process: All methods follow the standard two-stage training protocol commonly used in continual learning. Based on the Q-matrix, items are divided into mutually exclusive old and new sets. Old items involve only previously learned knowledge concepts, whereas new items may involve both old and newly introduced concepts, thereby establishing clear boundaries for incremental learning. In Phase 1 (Foundation Training), the model is trained on old items within the historical item–concept space ℐold×𝒦old\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{old}}\times\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{old}}. In Phase 2 (Incremental Training), the model is initialized from the foundation model and incrementally trained on new items after expanding to (ℐold∪Δ​ℐ)×(𝒦old∪Δ​𝒦)\left(\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{old}}\cup\Delta\mathcal{I}\right)\times\left(\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{old}}\cup\Delta\mathcal{K}\right). After incremental training, each model is evaluated once on separate old-item and new-item test sets. We use the checkpoint obtained at convergence for each of the ten random seeds and report the average performance across all ten runs. Old-item metrics measure retention after incremental learning, whereas new-item metrics measure adaptation to newly introduced items. In addition, G-NCDM serves as the anchor baseline (Li et al., 2026) and is evaluated only on the old-item test set.

Baselines:We compare CLEAN with six representative baselines: Full-Replay Oracle, EWC, DER++, C-LoRA, X-DER, and ICD (Tong et al., 2022; Kirkpatrick et al., 2017; Buzzega et al., 2020; Boschini et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025). These methods are divided into two groups. 1) Same-Backbone Comparison: Full-Replay Oracle, X-DER, C-LoRA, and CLEAN are implemented on the same G-NCDM backbone, enabling direct comparison of RD. X-DER is architecture-agnostic and can be faithfully applied to G-NCDM through sample replay, while C-LoRA performs low-rank updates on the shared backbone with the pre-trained parameters frozen. 2) Cross-Backbone Reference: EWC and DER++ assume fixed parameter dimensions and output spaces, whereas ICD was designed for its own diagnostic architecture. Adapting them to the expandable G-NCDM backbone would require additional structural modifications not included in the original methods. Therefore, EWC, DER++, and ICD are evaluated under their original implementations as cross-backbone references.

Evaluation Metrics: Following prior studies (Tong et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2020), we evaluate model performance indirectly through response prediction. We report ACC, F1, and RMSE separately on old and new items using the subscripts old\mathrm{old} and new\mathrm{new}. Higher ACC and F1, and lower RMSE indicate better performance. We also report ACCall\mathrm{ACC}_{\mathrm{all}} over all test interactions and RD for historical representation stability. Unless otherwise stated, ACC is used as the primary metric for statistical comparisons. Detailed metric results for each dataset are reported in Appendix A.2.

Implementation Details: We initialize the base-network weights using Xavier initialization (Glorot and Bengio, 2010) and the newly expanded CLEAN branches using micro-variance initialization with a scaling factor of 10−310^{-3}. All models are optimized using Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015) with a learning rate of 10−310^{-3} and the binary cross-entropy loss. Each model is trained for 25 epochs under Random-Split and User-Split. The residual mixing coefficient α\alpha is selected separately for each dataset and split. Under Random-Split, α\alpha is set to 0.20 for Math1 and 0.10 for both a0910 and Junyi. For a fair comparison, the hyperparameters of all baselines are selected based on the highest validation ACCall\mathrm{ACC}_{\mathrm{all}} . All models are implemented in PyTorch, and all experiments are conducted on a Linux server equipped with a single NVIDIA H100 GPU with 80 GB of memory, 22 CPU cores, and 240 GB of RAM. An anonymized implementation is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CLEAN-2E32/.

5.2. Experimental Results

The Random-Split setting ensures that each learner appears in the training, validation, and test sets. We adopt it as the primary setting because it provides a controlled evaluation of incremental prediction: the model must accommodate newly added items and knowledge concepts while continuing to predict responses for previously observed learners.

Overall Comparison. Table 1 reports ACCold\mathrm{ACC}_{\mathrm{old}}, ACCnew\mathrm{ACC}_{\mathrm{new}}, ACCall\mathrm{ACC}_{\mathrm{all}}, and Representation Drift (RD) on Junyi, ASSISTments a0910, and Math1. G-NCDM denotes the foundation-stage anchor trained only on old items. Across all three datasets, CLEAN-Full and CLEAN-LoRA exactly match the anchor in ACCold\mathrm{ACC}_{\mathrm{old}} and consistently achieve RD=0\mathrm{RD}=0, demonstrating that architectural isolation preserves the historical diagnostic subspace during incremental learning. On Junyi, CLEAN-Full achieves an ACCnew\mathrm{ACC}_{\mathrm{new}} of 74.53 and an ACCall\mathrm{ACC}_{\mathrm{all}} of 77.19, ranking second only to Full-Replay Oracle, which obtains 75.47 and 77.58, respectively. CLEAN-Full also outperforms all non-oracle baselines in overall accuracy. On ASSISTments a0910, CLEAN-Full achieves an ACCnew\mathrm{ACC}_{\mathrm{new}} of 72.21 and an ACCall\mathrm{ACC}_{\mathrm{all}} of 73.11, again ranking second only to Full-Replay Oracle and outperforming the remaining continual-learning baselines. On Math1, CLEAN-Full obtains an ACCnew\mathrm{ACC}_{\mathrm{new}} of 72.25 while exactly retaining the anchor-level ACCold\mathrm{ACC}_{\mathrm{old}} of 72.14. Although several baselines achieve higher new-item accuracy on Math1, CLEAN-Full provides a better balance between preserving historical representations and learning newly introduced items.

Psychometric Consistency. Figure 5 visualizes the AlignedUMAP (Dadu et al., 2023) projections of the old-concept trait subspace 𝜽old\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{old}} on Math1 before (t=0t=0) and after (t=1t=1) incremental learning. All four visualized methods use the same G-NCDM backbone, and each point is colored according to the learner’s observed accuracy on old items. For CLEAN-Full, the two embeddings perfectly overlap, preserving both the global U-shaped geometry and the accuracy gradient. This visual stability is consistent with its RD=0.00\mathrm{RD}=0.00 in Table 1. In contrast, Full-Replay Oracle and X-DER retain the general U-shaped structure but exhibit noticeable displacement after incremental learning. C-LoRA shows the greatest deformation, with initially fragmented clusters becoming diffuse and irregular after the update. These observations are consistent with their nonzero RD values. Among the four methods, only CLEAN-Full shows no observable displacement. These results show that CLEAN preserves the historical representation space through architectural isolation, with RD=0\mathrm{RD}=0 serving as a representation-level indicator of psychometric consistency. In the following subsection, the ablation study further indicates that Orthogonal Column Masking and Shared Bias Freezing are both required to retain anchor-level performance on old items in this setting.

Takeaway. Under the Random-Split setting, CLEAN achieves exact retention of the historical trait subspace, with RD=0\mathrm{RD}=0 and anchor-level ACCold\mathrm{ACC}_{\mathrm{old}} across all three datasets. CLEAN-Full ranks second only to Full-Replay Oracle on Junyi and ASSISTments a0910, while maintaining a competitive balance between stability and plasticity on Math1.

5.3. Ablation study

The conventional continual learning baselines in Table 1 alleviate forgetting but still exhibit nonzero Representation Drift (RD>0\mathrm{RD}>0). One way to achieve RD=0\mathrm{RD}=0 is PNN-style architectural isolation (Rusu et al., 2016), which freezes the historical subnet and adds a lateral branch for new concepts. In CLEAN, this setting corresponds to CLEAN w/o OCM and SBF, which retains the lateral GDF expansion but removes both Orthogonal Column Masking and Shared Bias Freezing. As a result, the historical aggregation weights and shared bias remain trainable, allowing incremental gradients to alter downstream representations. Based on the same backbone, we further evaluate the individual contributions of Orthogonal Column Masking and Shared Bias Freezing on ASSISTments 2009–2010 under the random-split setting, as reported in Table 2.

All ablation variants achieve RD=0\mathrm{RD}=0, showing that freezing the historical GDF is sufficient to preserve the historical trait subspace measured by RD. However, zero representation drift does not necessarily guarantee unchanged predictions on old items because the shared aggregation layer remains downstream of the frozen GDF. Removing Orthogonal Column Masking reduces ACCold\mathrm{ACC}_{\mathrm{old}} from 69.42 to 60.22 and F1old\mathrm{F1}_{\mathrm{old}} from 78.69 to 67.63, while increasing RMSEold\mathrm{RMSE}_{\mathrm{old}} from 45.64 to 48.78. Removing Shared Bias Freezing causes a larger decline, with ACCold\mathrm{ACC}_{\mathrm{old}} falling to 55.99, F1old\mathrm{F1}_{\mathrm{old}} to 60.29, and RMSEold\mathrm{RMSE}_{\mathrm{old}} rising to 49.53. When both mechanisms are removed in CLEAN w/o OCM, the degradation is most severe: ACCold\mathrm{ACC}_{\mathrm{old}} drops to 44.46, F1old\mathrm{F1}_{\mathrm{old}} to 38.06, and RMSEold\mathrm{RMSE}_{\mathrm{old}} increases to 54.73. By contrast, the new-item metrics vary only moderately across the variants, indicating that these two mechanisms primarily protect historical predictive pathways rather than improve adaptation to new items. Therefore, freezing the GDF alone is insufficient, and preserving the historical aggregation subspace requires both Orthogonal Column Masking and Shared Bias Freezing. Because RD measures only the GDF-level historical trait subspace, it cannot capture downstream prediction drift. To visualize such prediction-level drift, Figure 6 presents the AlignedUMAP embeddings of the old-item prediction vectors 𝐲old\mathbf{y}_{\mathrm{old}} before and after incremental learning.

6. CONCLUSION

In this study, we introduced CLEAN, an incremental cognitive diagnosis framework that encodes psychometric consistency as a hard architectural constraint. By combining strict topological bipartition, frozen historical GDFs, orthogonal column masking, and bias freezing, CLEAN preserves historical diagnostic outputs pointwise without replaying old responses, while its expandable full-rank and low-rank branches retain strong plasticity for newly introduced concepts. Experiments on Math1, Junyi, and ASSISTments, representing dense, moderately sparse, and highly sparse response settings, respectively, show that CLEAN achieves zero representation drift (RD=0\mathrm{RD}=0) and maintains anchor-level performance on old items. CLEAN also achieves performance competitive with or superior to that of existing continual learning baselines. Under concept-space expansion, these results establish architectural isolation as an effective solution for eliminating catastrophic forgetting while maintaining psychometric consistency. Future work will extend CLEAN to multi-stage continual streams and investigate long-horizon consistency, cumulative capacity growth, and adaptation under repeated item and concept expansion.

Appendix A Appendix

A.1. User-Split Results

Table 3 reports the response-prediction results on ASSISTments 2009–2010 under the User-Split setting, in which the training, validation, and test sets contain disjoint groups of learners. This protocol evaluates each model’s ability to diagnose previously unseen learners from a limited set of support responses. The table also includes the original C-LoRA configuration as a reference for comparison with the G-NCDM-based variant used in our experiments. The results show that replacing the original backbone with G-NCDM does not by itself improve predictive performance. C-LoRA-GNCDM generally performs worse than the original C-LoRA on both old and new items, although their RMSEnew\mathrm{RMSE}_{\mathrm{new}} values are nearly identical.

All methods use the same support–query partition and are evaluated on the same held-out query interactions. G-NCDM-based methods infer learner traits directly from the support responses, whereas the transductive baselines use these responses to optimize learner-specific embeddings, and ICD incorporates the support interactions into its neighborhood graph. Therefore, although the methods process support information differently, their predictive performance is measured on the same query set.

CLEAN-LoRA achieves the best predictive performance on new items, with ACCnew=69.92\mathrm{ACC}_{\mathrm{new}}=69.92, F1new=78.58\mathrm{F1}_{\mathrm{new}}=78.58, and RMSEnew=44.76\mathrm{RMSE}_{\mathrm{new}}=44.76, while maintaining zero representation drift on historical concepts (RD=0.00\mathrm{RD}=0.00). It also exactly preserves the anchor-level performance on old items, achieving ACCold=70.24\mathrm{ACC}_{\mathrm{old}}=70.24, F1old=79.65\mathrm{F1}_{\mathrm{old}}=79.65, and RMSEold=45.22\mathrm{RMSE}_{\mathrm{old}}=45.22. These results indicate that freezing the historical GDF preserves the existing diagnostic space without preventing adaptation to newly introduced items.

Among the non-CLEAN baselines, Full-Replay Oracle achieves an ACCnew\mathrm{ACC}_{\mathrm{new}} of 67.82, which is 2.10 percentage points lower than that of CLEAN-LoRA, while producing nonzero representation drift (RD=3.44\mathrm{RD}=3.44). EWC, DER++, C-LoRA, X-DER, C-LoRA-GNCDM, and ICD also exhibit nonzero representation drift and generally weaker predictive performance on new items. In particular, the larger drift observed for DER++, C-LoRA, and ICD suggests that replay, parameter-efficient updating, and graph-based adaptation do not by themselves guarantee the stability of the historical diagnostic space.

Overall, these results provide additional evidence that CLEAN-LoRA achieves a favorable stability–plasticity trade-off for previously unseen learners under limited-support conditions. It preserves historical representations and old-item predictive performance while maintaining strong adaptability to newly introduced items.

A.2. Detailed Metric Results on Each Dataset

Tables 4– 6 report the detailed ACC, F1, RMSE, and RD results on Junyi-Random, ASSISTments a0910, and Math1, respectively. Across all three datasets, CLEAN-Full and CLEAN-LoRA exactly match the G-NCDM anchor in ACCold\mathrm{ACC}_{\mathrm{old}}, F1old\mathrm{F1}_{\mathrm{old}}, and RMSEold\mathrm{RMSE}_{\mathrm{old}}, while consistently achieving RD=0\mathrm{RD}=0. This confirms that CLEAN preserves both historical trait representations and old-item prediction performance after incremental updates. On Junyi-Random, CLEAN-Full achieves an ACCnew\mathrm{ACC}_{\mathrm{new}} of 74.53, an F1new\mathrm{F1}_{\mathrm{new}} of 81.10, and an RMSEnew\mathrm{RMSE}_{\mathrm{new}} of 41.83, remaining close to the Full-Replay Oracle without replaying historical data. A similar pattern is observed on ASSISTments a0910, where CLEAN-Full obtains 72.21, 79.61, and 43.45 for the three new-item metrics, respectively. On Math1, replay-based methods achieve stronger new-item performance, whereas CLEAN-Full retains the anchor-level old-item metrics with zero representation drift. Overall, the detailed results demonstrate that CLEAN provides strict historical stability across datasets while maintaining competitive adaptability to newly introduced items and concepts.

A.3. Sensitivity Analysis of the Residual Mixing Coefficient α\alpha

The coefficient α\alpha balances the implicitly learned representation and the explicitly extracted QQ-matrix representation. A smaller α\alpha places greater weight on θimp\theta^{\mathrm{imp}}, whereas a larger α\alpha emphasizes θexp\theta^{\mathrm{exp}}. We evaluate different values of under the Random-Split setting. As shown in the left panel of Figure  7, the mean validation accuracy on Math1 first increases and then decreases, reaching its maximum at α\alpha=0.2. For Junyi and ASSIST09-10, the best performance is achieved at α\alpha=0.1, after which accuracy declines as increases. A similar downward trend is observed in accuracy on incremental data, particularly at large values of . These results indicate that excessive reliance on foundation-stage information limits the model’s ability to adapt to incremental data. Although the optimal value varies across datasets, relatively small values of consistently provide a better trade-off between retaining previously learned information and incorporating new information. Based on the validation results, we set α\alpha=0.2 for Math1 and α\alpha=0.1 for Junyi and ASSIST09-10.
